title: The Bell That Rang for the Sea
summary: Beneath the harbor of Saltmarrow lies a drowned town, and a bell that still rings on stormy nights. When Wick learns the bell can call the drowned back to shore, he wants to ring it for his lost father — until he understands what comes back is not who went under.

chapters.title: The Drowned Town
chapters.body:
Everyone in Saltmarrow knew there was a town under the water.

You could see it on a calm day, if you rowed out past the harbor mouth and looked down through the clear cold green: rooftops, a street, the pale finger of a church tower, all of it drowned generations ago when the sea rose in one terrible night and swallowed old Saltmarrow whole. The town had simply rebuilt itself higher up the hill, and the people learned to live with a graveyard of houses lying beneath their boats.

And on stormy nights, when the wind came hard from the water, you could hear it: a bell. Deep and slow and green-sounding, rolling up from the drowned church tower under the waves, tolling in the dark. The old folk said it was just the current moving the old bell, a dead thing swung by the sea. But they said it in a certain way, not quite meeting your eyes, and they always made sure the children were inside and the shutters closed before the bell began.

Wick was twelve, and he had a reason to listen to that bell more closely than most. A year ago, his father had gone out with the fishing fleet on a clear morning, and a squall had come up from nowhere by afternoon, and three boats had not come home. They never found the men. The sea had simply taken them, the way it had taken old Saltmarrow, and Wick's father was down there now, somewhere in the cold green dark, with the drowned town and the drowned bell.

Wick could not make peace with it. A death with a grave is a hard thing, but a death with no grave — no body, no place to stand and say goodbye — is a wound that won't close, because part of you never stops waiting. Every clear day, Wick rowed out and looked down at the drowned rooftops, as if he might see his father walking one of those streets. Every stormy night, he pressed his ear to the shutters and listened to the bell, and wondered.

It was the old lamp-woman, Merla, who told him the truth, because she was too old to be careful anymore and thought the boy deserved to know.

"That bell doesn't ring by accident, child," she said, her voice like dry reeds. "It's a calling bell. The old folk sank it on purpose, long ago, before the town went under. A bell to call the lost home from the sea." She looked at him with cloudy eyes. "They say if you row out over the drowned church on a storm night, and you ring that bell yourself — three times, with your own hand on the rope — it calls back whoever the sea has taken. Calls them up out of the green and back to the shore." She paused. "But they stopped ringing it, Wick. A hundred years ago, they stopped. And they sank the rope so deep no one could reach it easy. There's a reason they stopped. There's always a reason."

But Wick had stopped listening after calls them back. Because his father was down there. And a bell that could call him home was the only thing in a year that had felt like hope.

chapters.title: What Comes Up From the Green
chapters.body:
Wick found the rope on the third storm.

It took him that long — three nights of rowing out alone over the drowned church while the wind screamed and his mother thought he was asleep, three nights of diving down into the black-green cold, lungs burning, feeling along the slick stones of the sunken tower. On the third night his fingers closed on it: an old rope, furred with weed, running down into the dark from the mouth of the drowned bell. The bell the old folk had sunk deep and left alone for a hundred years.

Wick clung to his little boat, gasping, the rope in his frozen hands, the storm howling around him. And he thought of his father, and he pulled.

The bell rang.

He felt it more than heard it — a deep green shudder that came up through the rope and the water and into his bones, rolling out through the drowned town below, into every cold flooded street. Once.

He pulled again. Twice. The sound rolled out further, and something in the dark water below him seemed to stir, to turn, to notice.

His hands shook on the rope. Every instinct told him to stop, to drop it, to row home. Merla's voice was in his head — there's a reason they stopped. But his father was down there. He pulled a third time.

Three.

And the sea went still.

The storm did not stop, but the water around his boat went flat and quiet, as if something enormous below were holding it steady. And then, in the green depths, Wick saw lights — pale, drifting, cold blue lights, rising slowly from the drowned streets. Dozens of them. Rising toward the surface. Rising toward him.

The first broke the water beside his boat, and Wick's heart leapt and then froze.

It was a man. Or the shape of a man — pale and glistening and wrong, water streaming from him though he did not seem to breathe, his eyes the flat cold blue of the deep lights. He was one of the drowned. And he was smiling, a slow gentle smile, and he reached a dripping hand toward Wick's boat.

"You called," the drowned man said, and his voice was the sound of water moving through a flooded house. "How kind. It's so cold down there. So dark. We've waited so long for someone to call us up."

More of them surfaced around the boat — pale shapes, cold lights, dripping smiles — and Wick understood, with a horror that went deeper than the cold, why the old folk had stopped ringing the bell. It did call the drowned back. But the drowned who came back were not the people who went under. They were what the cold green dark had made of them over the long years — hollow, hungry, wearing the shapes of the lost like borrowed coats, reaching for the warmth and the life of the boy who'd been foolish enough to call.

And then, among the pale wrong faces, Wick saw one he knew. Thinner than in life, paler, his eyes gone the flat blue of the deep — but his father's face. Rising from the green with the same slow, hungry, borrowed smile as the others.

"Wick," the thing with his father's face said, in a voice almost like his father's, almost. "My boy. You came for me. Help me into the boat, son. It's so cold. Take my hand."

And Wick, weeping, reached for it — because he had wanted so badly, for a whole year, to take his father's hand one more time.

chapters.title: The Goodbye That Was Never Said
chapters.body:
Wick's hand was almost touching the cold dripping fingers when the thing's smile widened just a little too far — wider than his father's smile had ever gone — and Wick stopped.

Because his father, his real father, had a particular way of saying his name. A warmth in it, a little roughness, a laugh always half-hidden underneath. And this — this pale rising thing said Wick with the shape of the word but none of the warmth, the way the borrowed mirror had once smiled with the shape of a face and none of the person. Wick had spent a year aching for his father. He knew the difference between the man and a cold thing wearing the man's face. And this was not his father. His father was gone. This was only the green dark, hungry, reaching up through a beloved shape to pull a warm living boy down into the cold.

"You're not him," Wick said, and his voice broke on it, because saying it aloud meant admitting the thing he'd spent a year refusing to admit. His father was not coming back. Not up the bell-rope, not out of the green, not ever. Dead was dead, and no calling bell could undo it — it could only dredge up a cold mockery wearing a stolen face.

The thing's smile faltered. "I am your father," it said, in the almost-voice. "Take my hand. You called me. You want me back. Help me into the boat."

"I do want you back," Wick said, sobbing now, the storm whipping the tears from his face. "I want him back so much I dove into the dark three nights to find a way. But you're not him. He's gone. And you — you're just the cold, pretending, so I'll pull you up and you can take me down." He gripped the edge of the boat. "I won't. I won't trade the warm world for a fake of my dad. He wouldn't want that. He'd want me to go home."

The pale things hissed — a sound like a wave dragging back over stones — and the cold lights flared, and for a moment Wick thought they would swarm the boat and pull him under anyway. But he understood, now, the shape of what he had to do. The bell had called them up. Only the bell could send them down. And a calling bell, rung backward — rung to say not come home but rest — might close the door he had so foolishly opened.

He seized the weed-furred rope one more time. But this time, as he pulled, he did not ring the bell to call. He rang it to say goodbye — the goodbye he had never gotten to say, the goodbye with no grave, the goodbye a year overdue.

"Goodbye, Dad," he said, and pulled the rope. The bell tolled, deep and green. "I'm sorry I couldn't say it before. I'm sorry there was no place to stand and say it." He pulled again, weeping, the bell rolling out through the drowned town. "I loved you. I love you. And I'm going to live — a whole life — and carry you in it. But I have to let you go down. I have to let you rest."

The third toll rolled out across the still water, and the pale things began to sink. Not dragged, not banished — released. The cold lights dimmed and drifted down, back toward the drowned streets, back toward the green dark, one by one. And the last to sink was the thing that wore his father's face, and as it sank, just for a moment, the flat blue left its eyes, and something warmer flickered there — whether real or only Wick's wishing, he never knew — and the almost-voice said, so faint he barely caught it: "Good boy. Go home."

And then the green closed over it, and the sea was only the sea again, and the storm blew itself out toward the dawn.

Wick rowed home in the grey first light, emptied out and aching and, somehow, lighter than he'd been in a year. Because the wound of a death with no grave is that you never get to say goodbye — and he finally had. Not to his father, who was gone past all calling, but into the deep green dark where his father had gone, with his own hand on the old bell-rope and his own voice in the storm. It wasn't the goodbye he'd wanted. But it was a true one. And a true goodbye, he was learning, is the thing that finally lets a wound begin to close.

They never rang the calling bell again in Saltmarrow. Wick himself dove down one last calm day and cut the rope loose, and let it sink into the drowned church for good, so that no other grieving child would ever be tempted to call up what the cold green dark makes of the ones we've lost. But on stormy nights, when the deep bell still tolled — swung now only by the current, a dead thing moved by the sea — Wick would lie awake and listen, not with longing anymore, but with something like peace. It was just the bell. His father was resting. And Wick was alive, in the warm world, carrying him forward the only way the living ever can: not by pulling the dead back, but by remembering them, and letting them rest, and living on.
